breadseed-poppy.days_to_bloom: About 80 to 90 days from sowing to bloom.
breadseed-poppy.germination: Seed sprouts in 14 to 21 days at 60–65°F. Scatter it on the surface and do not cover it — the seed needs light.
breadseed-poppy.good_to_know: Breadseed poppy sows itself freely — leave a few dry pods standing and you will have plants again next year.
breadseed-poppy.growing: Full sun and soil that drains well. Once it is up and growing it asks for little.
breadseed-poppy.hardiness: Hardy annual — the foliage shrugs off light frosts.
breadseed-poppy.sowing: Direct sow in early spring, or in late summer and fall for earlier blooms. It makes a fragile taproot and hates being moved, so sow it where it will grow.
breadseed-poppy.spacing: Thin seedlings to 8 to 10 inches apart.
breadseed-poppy.transplanting: Do not transplant. Poppies grow a fragile taproot and take transplanting very poorly, so direct sowing is the way.

calendula.days_to_bloom: About 50 to 55 days from sowing to bloom.
calendula.germination: Seed sprouts in 7 to 14 days at about 70°F.
calendula.growing: Sun or part shade, in rich, well-drained soil. Calendula is frost-tolerant and keeps blooming late into fall.
calendula.hardiness: Annual — frost-tolerant; it blooms from summer right up to a heavy frost.
calendula.harvest_for_cutting: Cut flowers when they are about half open. The petals are edible — pull them from fully open flowers, but don't eat the green base or the centre of the flower.
calendula.sowing: Direct sow after the danger of frost, ¼ inch deep — direct sowing is the standard way. Make 2 or 3 sowings, 2 to 3 weeks apart, for a steady run of flowers.
calendula.transplanting: You can also start indoors 4 to 5 weeks before planting out, and move seedlings out around the last frost.

celosia.days_to_bloom: Plume types take about 85 to 100 days from sowing. Cockscomb types vary widely by variety, roughly 55 to 120 days.
celosia.germination: Seed sprouts in 8 to 14 days at 70–80°F. The seed needs light, so cover it only very lightly. Water from below, or mist, so the tiny seed isn't washed away.
celosia.good_to_know: Celosia sows itself in the garden — expect volunteers where heads ripened last year.
celosia.growing: Full sun and well-drained, moist, fertile soil. Pinch the growing tip at 6 to 12 inches tall on plume and crested types grown for many stems — but don't pinch the single-flower production types, which make one flower per plant.
celosia.hardiness: Annual — plant out after the danger of frost; it wants real warmth.
celosia.harvest_for_cutting: Cut fresh when the flowers are fully developed and the stem feels firm at the base of the bloom — they last 7 to 14 days in the vase. For drying, cut at the same stage, strip the leaves, and hang the stems in a dark, airy place.
celosia.sowing: Start indoors 6 to 8 weeks before planting out. Direct sowing only works where the season is long — sow ⅛ inch deep after the last frost.
celosia.transplanting: Grow seedlings warm, at about 63–68°F, harden them off, and move them out only after the danger of frost has passed. Cold weather and short days can make young plants flower too early, so don't rush them out.

cornflower.days_to_bloom: About 65 to 75 days from sowing to bloom.
cornflower.germination: Seed sprouts in 7 to 14 days at 60–65°F. Cover the seed lightly.
cornflower.good_to_know: Cornflower sows itself and naturalises easily — let a few heads ripen if you want it back next year.
cornflower.growing: Full sun. Cornflower tolerates poor soil and is an easy, low-fuss flower that brings in beneficial insects.
cornflower.hardiness: Hardy annual — frost-hardy; fall sowings can come through snow in mild climates.
cornflower.harvest_for_cutting: Cut fresh flowers when they are a quarter to half open. The petals are edible.
cornflower.sowing: Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked, ¼ inch deep — sow thinly, about 6 seeds to the foot, and keep the surface moist. You can also sow 2 to 4 weeks before the last frost, or in fall in mild climates.
cornflower.spacing: Thin seedlings to 6 to 9 inches apart at the first true leaves.
cornflower.transplanting: Direct sowing is best. If you start indoors, sow 3 to 4 weeks before planting out and grow the seedlings cool, with nights around 50–55°F, so they build a good root ball.

cosmos.days_to_bloom: Cosmos bipinnatus takes about 90 to 110 days from sowing. Cosmos sulphureus is faster, at about 65 to 75 days.
cosmos.germination: Seed sprouts in 7 to 10 days at 68–72°F. Cover the seed lightly.
cosmos.growing: Full sun. Pinch young plants to make them branch, keep cutting or deadheading for flowers all summer, and give tall varieties some netting or support to lean on.
cosmos.harvest_for_cutting: Cut when the petals are just opening, before the flower flattens out.
cosmos.sowing: Start indoors 5 to 7 weeks before planting out, or direct sow after the last frost once the soil is above 60°F.
cosmos.spacing: Space plants 9 to 12 inches apart — wider spacing gives stronger, thicker stems.
cosmos.transplanting: Harden seedlings off and move them out after the danger of frost, spacing them 9 to 12 inches apart.

echinacea.days_to_bloom: Expect flowers in the second year — echinacea spends its first year building a strong root and crown.
echinacea.germination: Seed sprouts in 10 to 21 days at about 65–72°F. Sow ⅛ to ¼ inch deep.
echinacea.good_to_know: Leave the standing seed heads for the goldfinches — they love them — and expect seedlings to pop up around the parent plants.
echinacea.growing: Full sun, at least 6 hours a day, and soil that drains well. Once settled in, it handles drought well, and it sows itself freely.
echinacea.sowing: Start indoors in late winter, or sow outside in fall and let winter do the chilling for you. A stretch of cold, damp conditions in the fridge — 8 to 12 weeks — improves sprouting for spring sowing.
echinacea.transplanting: Start indoors 8 to 10 weeks before you want to plant out. Move plants outside after frost, once the soil has warmed.

larkspur.days_to_bloom: About 80 to 90 days from sowing to bloom.
larkspur.germination: Seed sprouts in 14 to 21 days at about 55°F, sown ¼ inch deep — it needs darkness. Chilling the seed in the fridge for 7 days before sowing improves sprouting.
larkspur.good_to_know: Every part of larkspur is poisonous, including the seed — keep it away from children and livestock.
larkspur.growing: Full sun, in rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil. Plants grow 3 to 4 feet tall and do best with support.
larkspur.hardiness: Annual — a cool-season flower; sow in fall in mild climates or early spring elsewhere.
larkspur.harvest_for_cutting: Cut fresh stems when 2 or 3 of the bottom flowers are open, up to about a third of the spike — expect 5 to 7 days in the vase. For dried flowers, cut when the flowers are open but before the petals drop.
larkspur.sowing: Direct sow in early spring, or in fall for blooms the next year. Seed sprouts poorly once the soil warms past 55°F, so sow early and cool.
larkspur.transplanting: Direct sowing works best. If you start indoors, sow 5 to 7 weeks before planting out, keep the seedlings cool at about 55°F, and move them out while the weather is still cool.

marigold.days_to_bloom: From sowing: about 50 days for French types, 60 days for signet (Gem) types, and 70 to 90 days for African types.
marigold.germination: Seed sprouts in 4 to 7 days at 75–80°F. Cover the seed lightly.
marigold.growing: Full sun. Marigolds are easy, steady bloomers from summer until frost.
marigold.hardiness: Annual — plant out after the danger of frost.
marigold.harvest_for_cutting: Cut when the flowers are fully open but the centres are still tight.
marigold.sowing: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before planting out — or 8 weeks ahead if you want them already in flower. Direct sowing ¼ inch deep works too.
marigold.spacing: Space French types 8 to 12 inches apart, Gem types about 12 inches, and African types 12 to 18 inches.
marigold.transplanting: Move seedlings out after the danger of frost has passed.

nigella.days_to_bloom: About 65 to 75 days from sowing to bloom.
nigella.germination: Seed sprouts in 10 to 14 days at 60–65°F. Sow about ⅛ inch deep.
nigella.good_to_know: Nigella sows itself readily — let a few pods ripen and drop and it will be back next year.
nigella.growing: Full sun. Nigella is easy and undemanding, and it sows itself around the garden.
nigella.harvest_for_cutting: Cut fresh stems when the buds are fully coloured, or the pods have just begun to form. For dried use, cut when the seed pods feel firm.
nigella.sowing: Direct sow in spring; it does best sown where it will grow. For a long run of flowers and pods, sow again every 2 to 3 weeks through spring.
nigella.spacing: Thin or space plants about 8 inches apart.
nigella.transplanting: It can be started indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost, but the taproot is touchy about being moved — handle seedlings gently, or just direct sow.

pincushion-flower.days_to_bloom: About 90 to 100 days from sowing to first flowers.
pincushion-flower.germination: Seed sprouts in 10 to 12 days at 65–70°F. Sow on the surface — the seed needs light to sprout.
pincushion-flower.growing: Full sun. Tall plants may need support to keep the stems straight for cutting.
pincushion-flower.hardiness: Annual — grown in a single season.
pincushion-flower.harvest_for_cutting: Cut when the flowers are almost fully open — about three-quarters open is the sweet spot. The green seed heads are good in arrangements too. Cut flowers last about 7 to 10 days in the vase.
pincushion-flower.sowing: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost, or direct sow about 2 weeks before the last frost. Make another planting every 2 to 3 weeks until midsummer for a steady run of flowers.
pincushion-flower.transplanting: Move seedlings out after the danger of frost has passed, spacing them 8 to 12 inches apart.

strawflower.days_to_bloom: About 75 to 85 days from sowing to bloom.
strawflower.germination: Seed sprouts in 7 to 10 days at 70–75°F. Do not cover the seed — it needs light. Water from below, or mist gently, so the tiny seeds don't wash away.
strawflower.good_to_know: Strawflower is an excellent dried flower — cut extra stems for winter arrangements.
strawflower.growing: Full sun and average soil with good drainage. Pinch young plants to make them branch, and tall plants may need support. Plants grow about 3 feet tall.
strawflower.hardiness: Annual — plant out after the danger of frost has passed.
strawflower.harvest_for_cutting: Cut when 2 or 3 layers of petals have opened, but before the flower opens all the way and shows its centre — pick on a bright morning. Over-ripe blooms fall apart when dried.
strawflower.sowing: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before planting out. Where summers are long, you can direct sow instead.
strawflower.transplanting: Harden seedlings off and move them out after the danger of frost has passed, spacing them 10 to 12 inches apart.

sunflower.days_to_bloom: From sowing: about 50 to 65 days for ProCut types, 60 to 70 days for Sunrich types, and 60 to 75 days for branching mixes.
sunflower.germination: Seed sprouts in 7 to 14 days at 70–75°F.
sunflower.good_to_know: Single-stem types make one flower per plant. Many cutting sunflowers are pollenless hybrids — nice for arrangements, but their seed won't grow true.
sunflower.growing: Full sun. Pinch branching varieties to encourage more stems — but never pinch single-stem types, or you will get poor blooms or none.
sunflower.hardiness: Annual — sow after the last frost.
sunflower.harvest_for_cutting: Cut when the colour first shows on the petals, or wait until the flower is almost fully open — either stage works for the vase.
sunflower.sowing: Direct sow after the last frost, ½ inch deep. Sow every 1 to 2 weeks for single-stem types, or every 2 to 3 weeks for branching types, to keep flowers coming.
sunflower.spacing: Spacing sets the bloom size: 4 to 6 inches apart for single-stem cutting flowers, 18 to 24 inches for branching types.
sunflower.transplanting: Direct sowing is best — sunflowers dislike root disturbance. If you start indoors, sow only 2 to 3 weeks before planting out and move them gently.

sweet-pea.days_to_bloom: About 75 to 85 days from sowing to first flowers.
sweet-pea.germination: Seed sprouts in 14 to 21 days at 55–65°F. Soaking the seed for 24 hours before sowing helps, and it should be sown ¼ to ½ inch deep — it needs darkness to sprout.
sweet-pea.good_to_know: The seeds and pods are poisonous — don't eat them, and keep them away from livestock.
sweet-pea.growing: Give them a trellis or netting to climb — support is a must. Pinch the growing tip when plants are 6 to 8 inches tall to make them branch.
sweet-pea.hardiness: Hardy annual — seedlings tolerate light frost.
sweet-pea.harvest_for_cutting: Cut in the coolest part of the day, when 2 or 3 flowers on the stem are open, and get the stems straight into water. Expect about 4 to 7 days in the vase. Keep picking — once the plants set seed in the heat, flowering stops.
sweet-pea.sowing: Sow indoors 4 to 5 weeks before you plant out, or direct sow early. Sweet peas need about 50 days of cool weather, under 60°F, to bloom well, so get them in early.
sweet-pea.transplanting: Plant seedlings out about a month before the last frost — they handle light frost fine. Set them 4 to 8 inches apart along their support.

zinnia.days_to_bloom: About 75 to 90 days from sowing to bloom.
zinnia.germination: Seed sprouts fast — 3 to 5 days at 80–85°F, or 5 to 7 days at 70–75°F. Cover the seed lightly; a heat mat helps.
zinnia.growing: Full sun and good air movement — space and airflow keep powdery mildew down.
zinnia.hardiness: Annual — plant out after frost; the first frost ends it.
zinnia.harvest_for_cutting: Cut as soon as the stem has firmed up: hold the stem about 8 inches below the bloom and give it a wiggle — if it flops, wait; if it stands stiff, cut. Zinnias don't open any further in the vase. Cut stems last about 7 to 10 days.
zinnia.sowing: Start indoors 4 weeks before planting out, or direct sow ¼ inch deep once the weather warms. Zinnias grow fast, so don't start them too early.
zinnia.transplanting: Move plants out after the danger of frost. Don't let seedlings sit and get root-bound, and handle the roots gently — rough transplanting can make double varieties throw single flowers.
